newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai finance minister to resign Thursday --adviser.
newsitem.headline: Thai finance minister to resign Thursday --adviser.

text.p: Embattled Thai finance minister Amnuay Viravan will submit his resignation to Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh on Thursday, his adviser said.
"We ... confirm that he (Amnuay) will resign and submit his resignation letter tomorrow," Pongsathorn Siriyothin told reporters late on Wednesday.
Pongsathorn's statement ended speculation, initially denied, that Amnuay would be leaving his job.
The rumours helped push the already-battered Thai bourse to a 98-month closing low. The Thai currency, the baht, also slipped on the news after earlier trading at a 16-year high offshore.
"This is to confirm rumours going around all day that the minister could hand in his resignation," Pongsathorn said.

Amnuay, who has been managing Thailand's ailing economy, has been a target of some political rivals within Chavalit's six-party coalition for some time, political sources said. His rivals have wanted him replaced because they were unhappy with his performance and style, they added.

Thailand has been wracked by a sharp economic downturn, high interest rates that have choked businesses, a plunging stock market, slowing consumer and investor spending and a baht that has been under speculative attack last month.
The unelected minister has been struggling to keep Thailand's ailing economy on a even keel since he became finance minister in the Chavalit administration.
The Thai stock index closed 2.97 percent or 14.78 points lower at 482.94, mainly on the Amnuay speculation.
In the two-tier baht market, the Thai currency, which soared to 22.300/500 in the morning on the offshore market, weakened to 23.850/950 late on Wednesday.
Financial experts in Thailand said they expected the stock and foreign exchange markets to slump further on Thursday on the news.

"The news of the resignation will accelerate the inevitable economic meltdown that Thailand seems to be facing. The stockmarket and the baht will fall on the news because of Amnuay's imminent resignation," said the head of a foreign investment bank, who declined to be identified.
He said the resignation was not unexpected as Amnuay had been under pressure from his political rivals to quit for sometime.
But he added that finding a suitable replacement for Amnuay would be a hard task for the government.
Earlier, the finance minister was enigmatic in his latest comments about his future. He said he had not submitted his resignation but had held talks with the Chavalit.
"I have not submitted my resignation letter ... because I have not finished typing it ... but I have talked to the prime minister," he told reporters.

Chavalit said separately that he had met Amnuay, whom he nominated to the finance minister's post when the ruling six-party coalition took power in December, but had not received any resignation letter from him.
"I have not received a resignation letter from the finance minister. But I already talked with him," the premier said.
Industry Minister Korn Dabbaransi, who is seen as an Amnuay rival, told reporters he saw no reason for Amnuay to resign despite differences with him on some tax issues.
Korn was in dispute with Amnuay over the raising of excise taxes on several consumer products and managed to convince the cabinet to reverse the decision.
He said the tax issue should not be taken as pressure for Amnuay to quit but, if there was any such pressure, it could be due to pressure from current economic problems.
